Whose Definition of Done? The Smart Refill Decision at Dalchini Pantry

Bengaluru, 15 September 2026

1. Opening

At 7.40 pm on 15 September 2026, Ishita Rao closed her laptop for a moment and looked out over Bellandur from Dalchini Pantry's eleventh-floor office. In fifteen hours she was due at a leadership sync with the founders, and she had one recommendation to make: should "Smart Refill" — the reorder-prediction feature her pod had spent the summer building — be declared done and enter the code freeze on Friday, 25 September, or should it be held back? The freeze mattered because whatever crossed it by Friday evening would ship inside the app's Diwali update on 20 October, timed to the company's biggest sales window and to a live demonstration in Dubai that her sales head had already promised a large prospective client. Ishita's engineering lead said the feature was done. Her QA lead in Pune said it was not. Both had evidence. She had until morning to decide whose definition would govern.

2. Company background

Dalchini Pantry was founded in Bengaluru in 2019 by two IIM Ahmedabad batchmates who wanted to sell whole spices, ground masalas, ghee, atta and dals with traceability back to the farmer-producer organisations in Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Kerala that supplied them — each pack carried a QR code showing its lot and harvest month. The brand grew through its own app and website and through listings on Blinkit, Zepto, Swiggy Instamart, Amazon and BigBasket, competing for shelf attention against Tata Consumer's Tata Sampann, ITC's Aashirvaad and Sunrise ranges, Everest and MDH. By FY26 Dalchini Pantry had reached ₹180 crore in net revenue, 40 lakh cumulative app downloads and 6 lakh monthly active households, but its quarterly repeat-purchase rate had plateaued at 38 percent — most households reordered only when a quick-commerce app nudged them, not because Dalchini's own channel reminded them first. Closing that gap, without paying performance-marketing fees on repeat orders the brand should have owned outright, was the strategic reason Smart Refill existed.

3. The situation

Smart Refill was scoped in June: using order history and household size, a model would predict when a family was likely to run low on staples like turmeric, red chilli powder, garam masala, toor dal or ghee, and send a WhatsApp nudge with a one-tap UPI Autopay reorder. The pod demoed a working version to leadership on 10 September. It looked clean — a single test account, one saved address, one masala running low, one tap to reorder. Engineering closed all fourteen Jira stories against it and, as far as Priya Suresh, the engineering lead in Bengaluru, was concerned, the feature was done.

Five days later, Kabir Malhotra, who leads QA out of Pune, sent Ishita a message that reframed the week. Running exploratory tests beyond the demo script, his team had found that Smart Refill had never been specified — let alone tested — for a household with more than one delivery address, for a recommended SKU that was out of stock and needed substitution, for a UPI Autopay mandate that failed and needed a retry path, or for the Gulf market catalogue that Dalchini's sales head was already promising a Dubai client. None of these gaps were bugs in the engineering sense; the acceptance-criteria document, written in June before Kabir's team joined the pod, simply never mentioned them. "Done," for engineering, had meant the happy path worked in staging. Nobody had written down what "done" meant for the cases outside it.

The gap was not only a QA finding. Meera Chandran, the data scientist in Toronto, had been quietly worried since August that the refill-prediction model performed unevenly: 71 percent precision for customers with three or more past orders, but only 52 percent for newer customers — who made up 48 percent of the active base. No minimum precision bar had ever been written into the story, so a 52-percent model was, technically, "deployed and logging correctly," which was the only bar anyone had asked of her. In Singapore, Farah Osman, who runs customer success, had already seen what an unbounded definition of done could cost: in an August pilot with 500 households, 9 percent complained about wrong-quantity nudges or duplicate autopay charges, each ticket costing her team roughly ₹450 in agent time and refunds. And in Berlin, the designer Lukas Brandt pointed out, not for the first time, that he had flagged missing error-state designs — substitution, mandate failure, address selection — in a July design review that never turned into follow-up tickets. Every one of these people had been doing their job correctly by their own definition of done. The definitions simply did not match.

4. The people

Priya Suresh — Engineering Lead, Bengaluru

Wants the freeze held to Friday

Her team hit every story in the original brief and built a clean, well-tested happy path. She is wary of scope being added "at the finish line" and worried that reopening the acceptance criteria now signals that engineering's word on "done" cannot be trusted.

Kabir Malhotra — QA Lead, Pune

Wants a written, signed-off Definition of Done before any freeze

His six-person team already runs the busiest weeks of the year during Diwali order volume. He does not want to be firefighting an unfinished feature in the same week, and he wants the four gaps he found named and owned, not waved through informally.

Meera Chandran — Data Scientist, Toronto

Wants a minimum precision bar attached to "done"

Nine and a half hours behind Bengaluru, she gets little live sync time with the pod. She is not against shipping — she wants the 52-percent-precision cohort either excluded from the first release or clearly flagged as lower confidence, rather than silently included.

Dave Ferraro — Head of International Sales, New Jersey

Wants the 20 October date kept, in any form

He has told Al Maya Supermarkets, the Dubai-based retail chain that stocks Dalchini's export range, that Smart Refill will be live for a trade-show demonstration on 18–20 October — a demo tied to a prospective ₹6 crore annual contract. A slipped date, to him, is a lost deal, not an engineering nuance.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 shows why the disagreement is not really about code quality: each function was, by its own lights, finished. Exhibit 2 shows the two things Ishita cannot avoid weighing against each other — committed revenue and marketing spend on one side, and a documented double-digit complaint rate and an unwritten precision bar on the other. Exhibit 3 shows how little slack sits between Kabir's finding and the freeze: nine days, with the Al Maya demo and the Diwali update locked four weeks after that.

6. The options

Option A — Ship as demoed, on schedule

Declare Smart Refill done against the original happy-path criteria, enter the freeze Friday, and launch on 20 October across the full base, including the Al Maya catalogue. This protects the ₹85 lakh in booked media spend and the Al Maya demo date outright. Its cost is that it ships knowingly incomplete: the four gaps Kabir found and the precision gap Meera found reach 6 lakh households, including the 48 percent with the least accurate predictions, during Dalchini's highest-order-volume week.

Option B — Hold the feature and rescope properly

Pull Smart Refill from the freeze, write a complete Definition of Done covering all four gaps and a minimum precision bar, and re-plan for a clean release roughly three weeks after Diwali. This is the lowest-risk option for quality, but it forfeits the festive window entirely, strands the ₹85 lakh already committed to the 20 October campaign, and very likely costs the Al Maya trade-show slot — Dave believes a missed date there effectively kills the ₹6 crore deal rather than merely delaying it.

Option C — Ship a bounded release, with the boundary as the Definition of Done

Launch on 20 October, but only to the tenured cohort (≥3 orders, single address, India, UPI Autopay) where the model's precision is 71 percent and the tested path holds — roughly 20 percent of MAU. Give Al Maya a live but ops-assisted pilot: the untested substitution and retry cases are handled manually by Farah's team for the first month rather than automated. Write down, before the freeze, exactly what "done" means for this bounded release and what remains to be built — multi-address support, substitution logic, retry flow, full GCC catalogue — as a named follow-up sprint before the rollout percentage is raised. This captures most of the festive upside and keeps the Al Maya date, at the cost of extra support staffing over Diwali and the discipline of not quietly widening the rollout before phase two is actually finished.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Where, in the process from June's scoping to the 10 September demo, should the gap in Smart Refill's Definition of Done have been caught — and whose responsibility was it to catch it?
  2. How should Ishita weigh the ₹6 crore Al Maya opportunity and the ₹85 lakh already spent against Meera's precision numbers and Farah's 9 percent pilot complaint rate?
  3. Engineering, QA, data science and sales each have a defensible definition of "done" in Exhibit 1. How should Ishita reconcile them into one that leadership can act on tomorrow?
  4. Which of the three options should Ishita recommend, and what would she need from Priya, Kabir, Meera and Dave to make that option hold once the freeze passes?

8. A note for the learner

This case turns on a single, ordinary failure: nobody agreed what "done" meant before the work started. Engineering's version — stories closed, happy path demoed — is not wrong; it is simply incomplete, because a Definition of Done is not one team's checklist but acceptance criteria plus the quality and release checks every function downstream depends on. When that agreement is missing at the start, it does not disappear — it resurfaces later, as a disagreement at the worst possible moment, dressed up as a personality clash between "QA being difficult" and "engineering moving too fast." Kabir was not adding scope on 15 September; he was pointing out that scope was never fully written down.

A well-reasoned answer here does not pick the option with no downside — there isn't one — it picks the option whose downside the team can name, staff for, and recover from, and it uses the moment to fix the underlying process, not just this release. Option A pretends the gaps do not matter and ships that pretence into the noisiest week of the year. Option B pretends timing does not matter and gives up a real, dated commercial opportunity to do so. Option C is the defensible path: it makes the Definition of Done explicit and tiered — done enough for a bounded, well-understood cohort now, with a second, harder Definition of Done named and scheduled for the rest — rather than treating "done" as a single, all-or-nothing state discovered at the deadline. That is also the deeper lesson this topic unlocks: real product organisations do not eliminate quality trade-offs, they negotiate quality bars and cut lines deliberately, in the open, before the freeze — not silently, after it. The value of the practice is not in agile ceremony for its own sake; a team can hold this conversation in one honest half-hour meeting. What matters is that the conversation happens before the sprint, not after the complaints.

Forty-Two Definitions of Done: The Release 8.0 Decision at Aarsi Systems

Pune, Sunday 20 September 2026

1. The night before

The Baner office was empty except for the security guard and a cleaning trolley parked outside the demo room. Revati Deshmukh, Vice President of Product at Aarsi Systems, had been at her desk since four, working on eleven slides she had already rewritten twice. At nine the next morning the board would meet in Mumbai, and the second item on the agenda was hers: Release 8.0 — acceptance status and recommendation.

Two things were entangled in that line, and Revati had not yet found a way to separate them. The first was narrow and dated. Aarsi's identity-verification SDK, embedded inside the apps of banks, NBFCs and insurers, had shipped a release candidate on 2 September carrying its first on-device face-match engine, built under the internal codename Sheesha. A top-five private-sector bank had contracted for it; acceptance by 31 October released ₹4.2 crore, and every month past that date cost Aarsi ₹35 lakh in delivery credits. Aarsi's own engineering checklist said 8.0 was done. The bank's contract said done meant something else, and part of that something else — an independent security audit of the on-device model — could not be scheduled before the second week of November.

The second thing was not dated at all, which was why it was harder. Anirudh Bhatkal, the co-founder and CTO, had circulated a two-page note on Thursday proposing that Aarsi adopt a single, company-wide Definition of Done and refuse, from the next renewal cycle, any contract whose acceptance annexure contradicted it. He wanted Revati to endorse it at the board. She had spent Saturday reading the annexures. There were forty-two of them, no two the same, and eleven of them were the reason Aarsi had revenue at all.

2. Company background

Aarsi Systems was founded in Pune in 2017 by Anirudh Bhatkal and Sameera Kulkarni, both formerly of a Pune payments processor, on the premise that every regulated Indian company would soon need to verify a stranger's identity in under ninety seconds, and almost none of them would want to build the machinery themselves. The company's SDK sat inside the customer's own app: document capture and OCR for PAN and Aadhaar offline XML, DigiLocker fetch, liveness detection, face match against the document photograph, and an auditable event log that a compliance officer could export.

The constraining decision came early. In 2019, chasing its first enterprise logo — a Chennai-headquartered NBFC in two-wheeler finance — Aarsi agreed to the client's draft contract without negotiating Annexure C, headed Acceptance Criteria and Certification. Annexure C made payment contingent not on Aarsi's delivery but on three client-side events: the NBFC's own user-acceptance testing, a certificate from an independent security auditor of the client's choosing, and written sign-off by the client's compliance head. Aarsi signed because the alternative was no logo.

The deal closed in eleven weeks instead of the usual twenty-six, and sales drew the obvious lesson. Over the next six years, some version of Annexure C went into every enterprise contract, edited by whichever client's legal team happened to be on the other side. By FY26, Aarsi had 61 enterprise clients, ₹168 crore of revenue and, in Revati's Saturday count, 42 distinct contractual definitions of done: 17 requiring a third-party security audit, 9 requiring the client's own regression pack to pass on the client's own devices, 6 pinning acceptance to the wording of a named regulatory circular, and one — the oldest — requiring a wet-signed certificate from a compliance officer who had left that company in 2023.

3. The industry

India's digital-onboarding market was created by regulation and is still shaped by it. The RBI's video-KYC provisions, the CKYC registry, UIDAI's offline Aadhaar XML, DigiLocker, and the account-aggregator framework under Sahamati each defined what a verification had to produce; the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 then defined what could be kept afterwards, and for how long. SEBI's onboarding norms governed the broking clients; the IRDAI norms governed the insurers. None of these frameworks used the word "done", but each of them decided, in practice, whether a release could go live.

The competitive field was crowded and credible — Signzy, IDfy, HyperVerge, Perfios and Karza all sold adjacent capability, and the large system integrators bundled verification into digital-lending programmes for banks. Aarsi's differentiation had always been narrow and defensible: the cleanest audit trail in the market, and an SDK that added under 9 MB to a client's app. The on-device model in 8.0 was meant to extend that. Running face match on the handset rather than on Aarsi's servers cut median verification time from 41 seconds to 12, cut cloud inference cost by roughly ₹1.9 per verification at a run rate of 34 lakh verifications a month, and — the argument Zoya Rahman made most often — meant the selfie never left the device, which simplified a great deal of DPDP-related paperwork for every client at once.

Aarsi's exposure was not only Indian. Since 2023 the SDK had been deployed by Qandeel Exchange LLC, a Dubai-headquartered remittance house serving the Gulf's South Asian workforce, whose onboarding ran under UAE Central Bank rules, on Emirates ID rather than Aadhaar, and in five languages. Qandeel represented ₹9.6 crore of annual contract value, Aarsi's second-largest single relationship, and its acceptance annexure was the only one drafted under DIFC law.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

The 8.0 programme began in February 2026 with a one-page brief and a belief that the hard part was the model. Nandita Basu's team in Toronto delivered a quantised face-match network in May that ran in 380 milliseconds on mid-tier Android hardware, and the demo to the leadership team on 4 June was, by every account, the best internal demo the company had ever given.

Through June and July the pod worked to Aarsi's engineering Definition of Done — a checklist Sneha Iyer's group in Hyderabad had written in 2022 and genuinely respected: unit coverage above 80 percent, no open blockers, integration tests green on the reference app, SDK size within budget, release notes published, and the audit-log schema versioned. On 2 September, 8.0-RC1 met every line of it. Sneha declared the release done and Tanmay Ghosh's release-engineering group in Kolkata cut the artefact.

Three things then turned out to be wrong, in ascending order of inconvenience.

First, on 8 September, the bank's programme office sent its integration test plan for the first time. It contained a clause nobody at Aarsi had read in two years: because the face-match model would now execute inside the bank's application on the customer's handset, the bank's information-security policy classified it as a change to the bank's own application binary, which required an independent audit by an empanelled assessor before production release. The bank's assessor had a slot on 9 November. The bank was not being difficult; its policy had said this since 2021, and Annexure C of Aarsi's contract with it said acceptance followed the audit.

Second, on 11 September, Rohan Pillai's customer-success team in Singapore reported that Qandeel's integration engineers had run 8.0-RC1 against their own device pool and recorded a match-failure rate of 6.8 percent, against 1.9 percent in Aarsi's test results. Qandeel's pool was heavy on older handsets bought in Sharjah's grey market; roughly a third of their applicants used devices below ₹10,000.

Third, and only on 17 September, Revati discovered that the three ambiguities were not independent. If Aarsi shipped 8.0 with the on-device model disabled by default — falling back to the server path for clients who had not completed their audits — then the release genuinely was done under 33 of the 42 annexures. But the flag that controlled it was read at SDK initialisation from Aarsi's configuration service, and four clients' annexures explicitly prohibited runtime behaviour changes delivered outside a version-controlled release. Making the fallback contractually clean for those four meant shipping two binaries, which the release checklist had never contemplated and which Tanmay estimated at six additional weeks of build and certification work.

5. The people

Anirudh Bhatkal — Co-founder and CTO, Bengaluru

Wants one company-wide Definition of Done, enforced from the next renewal cycle

His note argues that 42 definitions are 42 separate quality systems, none of them fully staffed, and that the company's engineering costs will keep rising faster than revenue until done means one thing. He is measured on gross margin, which fell from 71 to 64 percent over two years. What he does not say in the note is that the single DoD he has drafted is, almost line for line, Sneha's 2022 engineering checklist, and that it contains no clause about client-side audit, device coverage or regulatory version pinning.

Sneha Iyer — Director of Engineering, Hyderabad

Believes 8.0 is done and that the bank's audit is a delivery problem, not an engineering one

Her group has met its checklist on eleven consecutive releases and she can prove it. She is protective of that record, and of a team that has had no headcount added in five quarters. She has not said aloud that two of her four senior Android engineers have offers from larger firms, and that a six-week two-binary programme would, in her estimation, cost her at least one of them.

Tanmay Ghosh — Head of Quality and Release Engineering, Kolkata

Wants acceptance criteria written per contract before code starts, not after

He has maintained, privately, a spreadsheet mapping each client's annexure to the checks Aarsi actually runs; it has 42 rows and 14 columns and he has never shown it to the board. He believes the honest answer is that Aarsi has been accepting contractual obligations it does not test against, and has been lucky. He is also two months from a promotion decision and does not want the message to be that quality is the bottleneck.

Nandita Basu — Principal Data Scientist, Toronto

Wants the device-tier gap treated as a model problem with a timeline, not a blocker

Nine and a half hours behind Pune, she joins the pod's standup at 11 pm her time twice a week and otherwise works from written notes. She can lift low-end-device accuracy, she says, with four to six weeks of retraining on a properly sampled dataset — which Aarsi does not have and cannot buy quickly without DPDP-compliant consent. She does not volunteer that her original validation set was assembled from employee volunteers and a vendor panel, both in Indian metros.

Ines Haberl — Principal Designer, Berlin

Argues that "done" must include the failure experience, not just the success path

She has designed a retry-and-fallback flow for failed matches — three attempts, then a graceful hand-off to assisted video KYC — and has been asking since July for it to be treated as part of the release rather than as a follow-up. It sits in the backlog as a "UX enhancement". She suspects, but has not said, that if the fallback flow existed, a 6.8 percent match-failure rate would be a nuisance rather than an incident.

Rohan Pillai — Director of Customer Success, Singapore

Wants no release before Qandeel's numbers are explained

He owns renewals for APAC and the Gulf, including Qandeel's ₹9.6 crore, which comes up for renewal in March. His team absorbs the first three weeks after every release: last year that cost him 640 person-hours of unplanned work across four releases. He has not mentioned that Qandeel's CTO asked him, informally, whether Aarsi would consider an escrow arrangement for the SDK source — a question that usually precedes a vendor review.

Dev Ranganathan — SVP Enterprise Sales, New Jersey

Wants 8.0 accepted by 31 October, in whatever form makes that true

The ₹4.2 crore acceptance milestone falls in his Q3 number, and the bank's reference is written into two deals he is working in the US market for Indian-origin lenders. He argues, not unreasonably, that the audit is procedural and that the bank's own programme head has said informally that she can start the assessor process early if Aarsi gives her a frozen binary by 30 September. He does not say that he approved the last four acceptance annexures himself, without engineering review, to shorten the close.

Zoya Rahman — Head of Regulatory Affairs, Mumbai

Wants the DPDP advantage of on-device processing realised this financial year

She has told three clients' compliance heads that 8.0 removes the selfie from Aarsi's servers entirely, which is true of the on-device path and not true of the server fallback. If the fallback ships as the default, those conversations will have to be reopened. She has not circulated the fact that one client has already cited her assurance in an internal data-protection impact assessment.

Option A — Freeze on 30 September, hand the bank a binary, let acceptance follow

Ship 8.0 as it stands, with the on-device path enabled, give the bank's programme head the frozen artefact she has asked for, and let the 9 November audit run against a release already in her hands. Protects Dev's milestone timing and Zoya's DPDP position. Assumes the audit passes, that no finding requires a code change, and that the bank's UAT — not yet started, on devices Aarsi has never tested against — does not surface the cohort in Exhibit 5's empty row.

Option B — Ship with the server fallback as default, enable on-device per client

Makes 8.0 acceptable under 33 of 42 annexures immediately, and lets each client switch to on-device as their own audits complete. Costs the latency and cost advantages in the short term, reopens Zoya's conversations with three compliance heads, and breaks the four annexures that forbid runtime behaviour changes outside a version-controlled release — which puts Tanmay's two-binary estimate of six weeks back on the table.

Option C — Hold 8.0, fund the device-coverage work and Ines's fallback flow, re-release in November

Nandita's four-to-six weeks of retraining, a properly sampled dataset, the retry-and-hand-off flow, and a written per-contract acceptance map before release. Defers ₹4.2 crore, incurs up to ₹1.05 crore in credits, and asks a team with no added headcount in five quarters to absorb the delay.

Option D — Endorse Anirudh's single Definition of Done and treat 8.0 as its first test

Adopt one company-wide standard, refuse contradictory annexures from the next renewal cycle, and accept whatever that means for this release. Solves the structural problem Revati believes is real. Also means telling the board that a checklist written in Hyderabad in 2022 will now govern what a bank's information-security policy and the UAE Central Bank consider acceptable — and that eleven of the annexures Aarsi would be renegotiating account for ₹47 crore of revenue.

Revati is aware that all four options share an assumption: that "done" is a property of the software, discoverable by testing it hard enough. Tanmay's spreadsheet suggests something less comfortable — that at Aarsi, done has always been a property of an agreement signed by someone in sales, months before the code existed, and that the engineering checklist has been measuring a different thing entirely and calling it by the same name. She is also aware that the 31 October date, which frames every option as a trade against time, was itself written into Annexure C by a lawyer in 2021 and has never been tested with the client.

9. Deadline and hard constraints

  • Board meeting, Mumbai, 09.00 on Monday 21 September. Revati presents second.
  • ₹4.2 crore acceptance milestone releases only on the bank's written acceptance; 31 October, then ₹35 lakh per month in credits, capped at ₹1.05 crore.
  • The bank's empanelled assessor has one slot: 9 November. There is no second slot before January.
  • Qandeel's Schedule 4 requires a 30-day parallel run before production; the run has not started, and Qandeel's renewal review begins in March 2027.
  • Hiring freeze in engineering since Q1 FY26; no additional headcount approved for FY27 before the January review.
  • Any retraining dataset must satisfy DPDP consent requirements; Aarsi's existing validation consents permit internal model validation only.
  • Four annexures prohibit behaviour changes delivered outside a version-controlled release. Two-binary build and certification: six weeks, per Tanmay.
  • Gross margin guidance of 66 percent for FY27 was given to the board in July.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What, precisely, did Aarsi's engineering checklist measure on 2 September, and what did it not measure? Was Sneha Iyer right to declare 8.0 done?
  2. Exhibit 3 contains two defensible counts of the same thing that point in opposite directions. Which count should the board be shown, and what would you have to do before showing either?
  3. Exhibit 5's aggregate of 98.1 percent was accurate and was also, in effect, misleading. Where in the process from February to June should that have been caught, and by whom?
  4. Aarsi's 2019 decision to accept a client-drafted acceptance annexure bought speed and created forty-two definitions of done. Under what conditions was that a good trade, and when did it stop being one?
  5. Anirudh's single Definition of Done would be enforced by a company that does not control its clients' audits, devices or regulators. What would such a definition have to contain to survive contact with Exhibit 2 — and what would Aarsi have to give up to make it stick?
  6. What should Revati do on Monday morning: which option, on what evidence, and with what asked of Sneha, Tanmay, Nandita, Ines, Rohan, Dev and Zoya? What exactly should she say to the board about whether Release 8.0 is done — and about how Aarsi came to have forty-two answers to that question?

11. Late Sunday

At 11.20 pm Revati had the eleven slides open on one screen and Tanmay's spreadsheet on the other. She had written a recommendation at the top of slide nine three times and deleted it three times. Each version was defensible, and each one made a different person in her leadership team wrong in a way she could not yet justify.

Her phone showed a message from Nandita, sent at 1.48 pm in Toronto: Can pull a sampled set from the pilot clients if legal clears consent. Six weeks from a yes. Beneath it, one from Dev, sent from Newark twenty minutes later: Programme head is at her desk Monday. Tell me what to say. Neither of them was waiting for the same answer. Revati turned off the desk lamp, left both messages unread, and stood for a while at the window, looking at the Baner road below and thinking that the hardest number in all six exhibits was the one nobody had written down: the date on which anyone at Aarsi had last agreed, in advance and in writing, what finished meant.

Definition of Done

What does “done” mean on your team, and did anyone agree to it before the work started?

OneA sprint review in Bengaluru

On Tuesday 4 March 2025, at the sprint review of the Fulfilment squad at Vyapak Commerce Systems, a Bengaluru company selling order-management software to mid-market Indian retailers, the returns module was declared done. Priya Raghunathan, the squad’s engineering lead, demonstrated it on a staging environment: a store manager scanned a returned kurta, the system matched it to the original order, issued a credit note and updated stock. Seven stories, thirty-four points, all moved to the right-hand column of the board. Meera Krishnaswamy, the VP of Product, had a contract in her drawer that said this module would be live for Roopkatha Apparel — a 240-store chain and Vyapak’s largest account at ₹1.4 crore of annual recurring revenue — on 18 March, with a service-credit clause attached to the date.

Meera asked one question: if she rang the customer that afternoon and asked them to start using it tomorrow, what would happen? The answers came out slowly and in no particular order. The module had been built against a clean test tenant; there was no migration for the eleven customers who already had two years of return history in the old schema. Partial refunds — a customer returning two of three items — threw an unhandled exception that had been noted in a comment but not in the tracker. Nobody had written the operations runbook that Vyapak’s support team needed in order to answer a ticket about a stuck credit note. There were no alerts, so if credit notes silently stopped issuing at two in the morning, the first anyone would know was an angry call from a regional manager. The work was done in the sense that the code existed and demonstrated well. It was not done in the sense that mattered, which is that somebody else’s money could safely depend on it.

Meera’s problem was not that her engineers were careless. They were conscientious people who had genuinely believed, on the morning of 4 March, that they had finished. The problem was that nobody at Vyapak had ever written down what finishing meant, so each person had silently adopted their own definition, and each definition was locally reasonable. That gap — between seven private notions of “done” and one shared one — is what the definition of done exists to close.

TwoThe idea, stated precisely

A definition of done (DoD) is a short, written, team-wide list of conditions that every piece of work must satisfy before anyone is allowed to call it complete. It is agreed before the work starts, it applies to all work of that type rather than to any one item, and it is binary: a story either meets every condition or it is not done, with no partial credit.

The crucial distinction, and the one that separates people who understand the idea from people who merely use the phrase, is between the definition of done and acceptance criteria. Acceptance criteria are per-story and describe what this particular feature must do — “a partial return of two items from a three-item order issues a credit note for the value of those two items, net of any proportional discount.” They vary from story to story, and they are the subject of a separate topic that this one builds directly on. The definition of done is the opposite: it is constant across stories and describes what must be true of the work itself — tested, reviewed, migrated, instrumented, documented, deployable. Done is acceptance criteria plus the quality and release checks that apply to everything. A team can meet every acceptance criterion in a story and still be nowhere near done.

The idea comes out of the early Scrum and Extreme Programming communities. Kent Beck’s XP work in the late 1990s insisted that code was not finished until it was tested and integrated, and in 2002 William Wake popularised the phrase “done done” for exactly the gap Meera found. Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland made the term explicit in the Scrum Guide around 2010, and in the 2020 revision elevated it to one of three formal commitments, alongside the product goal and the sprint goal. The problem all of them were attacking is the same: the ninety-per-cent-done syndrome, in which a team reports steady progress for months and then discovers, in the fortnight before launch, that the residue of everything deferred has become a project of its own.

If Meera needed one sentence she could say in a steering meeting without sounding like a consultant, it is this: acceptance criteria tell us what this story must do; the definition of done tells us what must be true of any story before we are allowed to count it — and everything we skip is a debt that we will repay, with interest, at the worst possible moment.

ThreeHow it actually works

The mechanics are simple to describe and are routinely botched in the same three places, so it is worth walking through them with the Vyapak example in hand.

Step one: inventory what actually happens between “code compiles” and “a customer safely depends on it.” Meera ran this as a forty-minute exercise on 6 March. She asked the squad to reconstruct, from memory, everything that had had to be true for the last three features that reached production successfully. The list came to nineteen items: unit tests, a peer review, a schema migration script with a tested rollback, error handling for the partial cases, a support runbook, an alert on the critical path, a load check, a security review for anything touching payment data, release notes in Vyapak’s customer portal, and so on. Some of these had happened every time; some had happened once, under duress.

Step two: classify each item. Not everything on an inventory belongs in the definition of done. Some items are properly acceptance criteria for particular stories — the partial-refund arithmetic is a property of the returns feature, not of all features. Some are entry conditions rather than exit conditions and belong in a definition of ready, the parallel agreement about what must be true before work is pulled in. Some belong on a release checklist that runs once per release rather than once per story: Vyapak does not need to publish customer release notes for each of thirty-four points of work, but it does need to publish them before any release reaches Roopkatha Apparel.

Step three: filter the remaining candidates against three tests. A candidate belongs in the DoD only if it is universal (it makes sense for every story of this kind, not just the difficult ones), verifiable (somebody other than the author can tell in a minute or two whether it is true, which rules out items such as “code is clean”), and within the team’s control (the squad can complete it without waiting on a queue it does not own). The third filter is the one teams skip, and skipping it produces the most common pathology in the field: a DoD full of items that require an external security team or a shared QA group, which the squad then fails to meet every sprint through no fault of its own, which teaches everyone that the DoD is decorative.

Step four, usually left implicit: decide what happens to the things you deliberately leave out. The security review at Vyapak took nine working days and was run by a two-person team serving all six squads. It could not sit in a two-week DoD. The disciplined response is not to pretend it does not exist but to write it into an undone-work register: a visible list of the work that is known to be outstanding, with an owner and a date, so that the deferral is a decision rather than an accident. Large-Scale Scrum practitioners call the organisational version of this the “undone department,” and they mean it as a criticism — but a named debt is far safer than an unnamed one.

Step five: agree it before work starts, with the people who will be affected by it. This is what makes the DoD a commercial instrument rather than an engineering hygiene document. If Meera’s DoD includes a tested rollback migration, then her estimates include that work, and when a sales director asks for a date, the date carries it. If the DoD is agreed after the fact, it becomes a stick used in retrospectives rather than a constraint used in planning.

Step six: enforce it at the moment of counting, and record every exception. A story that misses one DoD item is not done; it does not move; its points are not claimed. The second half of this rule matters more than the first: every waiver should be recorded with who granted it and why. A team that cannot say how many waivers it issued last quarter does not have a definition of done, it has a wall poster.

FourA worked example: what the missing definition was costing

Meera wanted a number, because a number is what moves a discussion about engineering practice out of the realm of taste. She pulled the last five sprints of the Fulfilment squad — seven people, two-week sprints — and the stabilisation period that preceded the January release.

Exhibit 1 — Fulfilment squad, five sprints to the January 2025 release. Undone items are things a later, stricter definition of done would have required in-sprint; rework hours are the hours actually spent on them during stabilisation, from the squad’s own time records.

The arithmetic runs as follows. The squad claimed 210 points across five sprints, an apparent velocity of 42 points per sprint. But the release also consumed a three-week stabilisation period during which nothing new was built: 7 people × 15 working days × 6 productive hours = 630 hours, which matches the rework total in the table. Three weeks is 1.5 sprints. The true cost of those 210 points was therefore 6.5 sprints, not 5, giving a real velocity of 210 ÷ 6.5 = 32.3 points per sprint. The squad had been overstating its capacity by 42 ÷ 32.3 − 1 = 30 per cent for a year.

That overstatement is the expensive part, and not because of the hours. At a fully loaded cost of roughly ₹2,200 per engineer-hour, the 630 hours are about ₹13.9 lakh — real money, but survivable. The damage is that every commitment Vyapak made to a customer was built on a number that was 30 per cent optimistic, which is precisely why the Roopkatha Apparel date on 18 March was never achievable, and why nobody could see that in January.

Now change one input. Suppose Vyapak moves from quarterly releases to monthly ones, as its sales team has been asking. Under the loose definition of done, the stabilisation work does not scale down cleanly with the size of the release: roughly 40 per cent of it is fixed set-up — environment refresh, regression sweep, migration dry-run on eleven tenants — and only 60 per cent varies with content. Take the quarterly figure of 630 hours: the fixed portion is 252 hours and the variable portion is 378. Run three releases a quarter with a third of the content each, and you pay 3 × 252 = 756 fixed hours plus the same 378 variable hours, for 1,134 hours — an 80 per cent increase, about ₹24.9 lakh a quarter, for exactly the same features.

This is the reasoning that should decide how strict a definition of done ought to be, and it is worth stating as a general rule rather than a Vyapak-specific one. The value of in-sprint rigour rises with release frequency, because loose done-ness imposes a fixed tax per release. A team releasing twice a year can, rationally, run a thin DoD and a hardening phase. A team releasing weekly cannot: it must move almost everything into the DoD and automate the checking, or it will spend its life hardening. Meera’s squad wanted monthly releases, so the question of what belonged in the DoD had already been settled by that ambition.

FiveNuances the learner must acquire

The DoD is a floor, not a wish list

The most common failure of a first attempt is that it reads like a description of excellent engineering rather than a minimum bar. “Performance is acceptable,” “the design is elegant,” “test coverage is comprehensive” are aspirations, not conditions. A DoD item must be something the team is prepared to block a story on, every time, including at 6 p.m. on the last day of the sprint when a customer is waiting. If the team would not hold the line, the item does not belong. It is better to have a six-item DoD that is genuinely never violated than a twenty-item DoD that is waived twice a week.

Every item needs a named verifier and a verification cost

“Tested” is not an item; “unit tests for the new branches pass in the pipeline” is. The test is whether a second person can check it quickly. If verification takes half an hour per story, a seven-item DoD costs three and a half hours a story, which is more than some stories are worth, and the team will quietly stop checking. This is the strongest argument for automating DoD items into the build pipeline wherever possible: an automated check costs nothing per story and cannot be forgotten under pressure.

Done is not released, and released is not validated

A story that satisfies a good DoD is potentially releasable. Whether it is actually released is a separate decision involving customer readiness, training, contractual notice and commercial timing. And whether the released thing was worth building is a third question entirely, answered by instrumentation and outcome measurement, not by a checklist. A team can be perfectly disciplined about done and still build something nobody wants. The DoD protects against one class of failure — the invisible accumulation of unfinished work — and is silent about every other class.

Undone work is debt, and it compounds

The reason deferred work is worse than it looks is that the cost of finishing it rises with the time since it was written. The author forgets the context; other code is built on top of the unfinished version; a defect that would have cost twenty minutes to fix in the sprint costs hours once it is buried under four sprints of dependent changes, and costs a customer-facing incident if it escapes. This is why “we will clean it up later” is not a neutral scheduling choice but a financing decision taken at an unknown interest rate.

Items outside the team’s control belong somewhere else

If the DoD requires a sign-off from a shared platform group with a two-week queue, the squad’s done-ness is now a function of someone else’s backlog. The right move is either to negotiate the dependency away, or to move the item to the release checklist and the undone register where it is visible to the people who can actually resource it. Leaving it in the DoD guarantees chronic non-compliance and a slow erosion of the whole instrument.

It is a team agreement, but not only the team’s business

The team owns the content of its DoD, because the team is the only party that can honestly say what it takes to finish work well. But the organisation sets floors the team cannot lower: a company handling payment data under RBI supervision does not get to decide that a security review is optional. The useful mental model is that the organisation defines the non-negotiable minimum and the team defines everything above it — and the team may only ratchet upwards.

What it cannot tell you

A definition of done cannot tell you whether the work was worth doing, whether the estimate was right, whether the architecture will hold for another year, or whether the customer will adopt the feature. It cannot even tell you that the software is good; it can only tell you that a specific, agreed set of checks was performed. Teams that treat the DoD as a proxy for quality end up with a green board and an unhappy customer.

The questions a newcomer should ask first

Before relying on any team’s definition of done, four questions establish whether it is real. Who verifies each item, by name or by pipeline? What happened the last five times a story failed to meet it? When was it last changed, and what was added? And what is deliberately not on it, and where does that work live instead? A team that answers all four crisply has a working agreement. A team that produces a printed list and cannot answer the second question has a decoration.

SixHow it differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products, where releases are frequent and the cost of a small defect is usually low, the centre of gravity of the DoD shifts towards instrumentation and reversibility. The items that matter most are “the change is behind a flag that can be turned off without a deploy” and “the events needed to tell whether it worked are firing and verified in the analytics pipeline.” A consumer team that ships an experiment without working instrumentation has not saved time; it has spent two weeks to learn nothing, which is the most expensive outcome available.

In B2B and enterprise software of the sort Vyapak sells, the weight moves towards migration, backwards compatibility, documentation and support readiness. Customers run old versions, integrate through APIs that must not break, and reach a human being when something goes wrong. “The support runbook exists and a support engineer has read it” is a serious DoD item here and an odd one in consumer. Where the software is deployed on customer premises, as much enterprise software in India still is, the DoD must also account for configuration that differs per customer — and the honest answer is often that team-level done leaves a genuine remainder handled by an implementation team, which should be named as such rather than hidden.

In marketplaces, done has a supply side. A feature that changes how sellers are paid is not done when the code ships; it is done when the seller-operations team has an updated standard operating procedure, the field staff who onboard sellers know about it, and the two support scripts have been changed. Marketplace teams that define done purely in software terms reliably ship changes that the operations organisation cannot absorb, and the resulting mess looks like a product failure when it is a definition failure.

Stage matters too, though less than people claim. A ten-person company at pre-product-market fit, throwing away most of what it builds, should have a deliberately thin DoD — perhaps three items — because rigour applied to code that will be deleted in six weeks is waste. What it must not do is have no definition, because even there the difference between “it demos” and “a customer can use it unattended” is the difference between a real signal and a false one. A large company’s problem is the reverse: its DoD grows by accretion, each item added after an incident, until it is a twenty-four-point liturgy that everybody waives. Mature organisations prune it deliberately, usually by automating what can be automated and demoting the rest to a release checklist.

SevenCommon mistakes

The poster on the wall. The symptom, visible from outside, is that a printed definition of done hangs in the team area and no two people can recite the same three items from it. The underlying misunderstanding is that the DoD is a document rather than a behaviour — that writing it was the work. The cheapest diagnostic is to ask three team members separately, without warning, to name the items; if the lists differ, the agreement does not exist regardless of what is on the wall.

The aspirational list that is waived weekly. The symptom is a team that always meets its DoD except for the two or three items that are always the exception. The misunderstanding is confusing a standard with an ambition. The diagnostic is arithmetic: count waivers over the last six sprints and divide by stories completed. Anything above roughly one in ten means the DoD is describing a world the team does not live in, and the honest fix is to lower it to the truth and then ratchet it up deliberately.

Acceptance criteria smuggled into the DoD. The symptom is a definition of done containing feature behaviour — “credit notes are calculated correctly” — which cannot be universal because most stories have nothing to do with credit notes. The misunderstanding is treating done as a quality list rather than as the constant part of completion. The diagnostic is to read each item aloud against three unrelated stories from the backlog; if it does not make sense for all three, it is an acceptance criterion in the wrong place.

Done defined by the people who do not carry the consequence. The symptom is chronic disagreement at sprint review about whether work is finished, usually between engineering and support or operations. The misunderstanding is that done is an engineering concept. The diagnostic question is simple: for each item, who suffers if it is skipped? If the answer is a group that was not in the room when the DoD was written, the definition will not hold.

EightWhat good looks like

Consider the same March decision at a team that had done this properly. The definition of done is seven items long and fits on an index card, six of them checked automatically by the build pipeline and one — the support runbook — checked by a support engineer who attends sprint planning for fifteen minutes a fortnight. Because the definition existed before estimation, the returns module was sized at 52 points, not 34, and the difference was visible in October rather than in March. Because a tested migration was an item, the eleven existing tenants were in scope from the first story. Because the DoD was in the room during the commercial conversation, the date given to the customer was 8 April, and it held.

When the security review turned out to need nine days that would not fit, the squad did not quietly skip it. It went into the undone register with a named owner and a date, it was visible on the same board as everything else, and the release plan accounted for it. At the sprint review on 4 March, the demonstration was the same — a kurta scanned, a credit note issued — but the answer to Meera’s question, what happens if I ask the customer to use it tomorrow, would have been: they can, and here is the one thing we know is outstanding and when it lands.

NineWhat Meera decided

Meera did not ship on 18 March, and her reasoning is worth following because it was commercial rather than moral. She had two options for the missing work: do it now, or do it after the customer was live. Doing it after meant doing it under incident conditions on a chain with 240 stores and a service-credit clause — the most expensive hour in which to write a migration script. Doing it now cost three weeks of a date she had already given. She rang the customer on 7 March, offered a four-week slip with a phased rollout of twenty stores first, and used the conversation to establish something she had never had before: an agreed statement of what “live” would mean, item by item.

She then did the thing that mattered more than the release. On 12 March the squad agreed an eight-item definition of done, of which five were automated in the pipeline within a fortnight; the security review and the customer release notes moved to a release checklist; the performance budget for the returns query moved to the undone register with the platform team as owner and a June date. Velocity fell from a claimed 42 to a measured 31 points per sprint, which was not a decline but the first honest number Vyapak had ever had.

Two things are worth learning next. The first is acceptance criteria and error cases, which this topic sits directly on top of: a definition of done is only as good as the per-story criteria it supplements, and most of the defects Meera found were in the error cases nobody had written down. The second is negotiating quality bars and cut lines — because once a team has an honest definition of done, the real work begins, which is deciding with a customer or an executive what to cut when the date will not move. A DoD is precisely the instrument that makes that negotiation possible, since it converts “we could go faster if we tried” into “here is the specific check you are asking us to skip, and here is who will pay for it.”

Two questions to sit with. First: on the team you work with now, if you asked three people to write down what “done” means without conferring, how different would the three lists be — and which of the differences would have caused a customer-visible failure in the last quarter? Second: what is the single item you would most like to add to your team’s definition of done, and what would you have to give up — in velocity, in dates, in scope — to add it honestly rather than aspirationally?

Vyapak Commerce Systems and Roopkatha Apparel are fictional composites used for teaching. Figures are illustrative and internally consistent; they are not drawn from any real company’s records.

Definition of Done

An expert treatment: what “done” can mean, who gets to decide, what it costs to be strict, and where serious practitioners still disagree.

OneTwo decisions, two weeks apart

On Friday 12 September 2025, Aparna Sundaram, Head of Product at Palash Money, sat with a spreadsheet she had been avoiding. Palash is a Bengaluru consumer savings and lending application with 4.1 million monthly active users, most of them salaried people in tier-two cities who use it to round up transactions into a recurring deposit. In the first half of the financial year her three squads had run 41 experiments. The data team’s audit said that 13 of them — just under a third — had produced results nobody could use: event names that had been changed after the analysis plan was written, a user property that was never populated for Android, a funnel that double-counted because the same event fired on two screens. Each experiment had cost on average 9.5 engineer-days to build. Thirteen of them came to 124 engineer-days, roughly ₹22 lakh at Palash’s fully loaded rate, spent to learn nothing.

The remedy her principal engineer proposed was not a tooling project. It was three new lines in the squads’ definition of done: the analytics events for a change are verified end to end in the data warehouse before the story is counted; every user-facing change sits behind a flag whose off-switch has been exercised at least once in production; and a rollback path is demonstrated, not asserted. His estimate was that the three items would cost about nine per cent of throughput. Aparna had committed a roadmap to her board for the quarter on the old throughput. The decision in front of her was whether to make her teams slower in a measurable way in order to make them less wasteful in a way she could only estimate.

Two weeks earlier, on 26 August, Sunil Thakkar had been in a different kind of meeting in Pune. He is Director of Product at Anagha Insurance Technologies, which sells a policy administration suite to fourteen Indian insurers, most of it running in customers’ own data centres or private clouds, released on a quarterly cadence and operating in a market where the insurers themselves answer to the IRDAI. Anagha’s product squads had a definition of done; it ended at the boundary of the squad. Beyond that boundary sat the implementation organisation, which ran a regression pack of roughly 3,100 test cases against each customer’s configuration before an upgrade, because every insurer had a different product catalogue, commission structure and statutory reporting set-up.

The June upgrade at one of Anagha’s largest customers had surfaced 41 defects after go-live, nine of them severity-one, including a commission calculation that misapplied a slab for one channel. The remediation had consumed 340 person-days of Anagha’s implementation and support staff, and the customer had withheld ₹62 lakh of the annual maintenance fee pending a written plan. Sunil’s question was whether the product squads’ definition of done could honestly exclude customer-specific regression when the failures it was designed to catch were, in every commercial sense, product failures.

These two decisions look unrelated. They are the same decision. Both protagonists are being asked where to draw the line between work that must be complete before a team is permitted to say “done” and work that is legitimately somebody else’s, later. That line is the definition of done, and almost everything interesting about the topic is an argument about where to put it and who gets to move it.

TwoThe idea, its history and the schools that disagree

A definition of done is a pre-agreed, written, team-wide set of conditions that every increment of work must satisfy before it may be counted as complete. Three properties do the work in that sentence. It is pre-agreed, so it constrains estimates and commitments rather than merely judging them afterwards. It is team-wide, applying to all work of a kind rather than to a particular item — which is precisely what distinguishes it from acceptance criteria, the per-story statements of what a specific feature must do. And it is binary: the increment meets all of it, or it is not done. Done is acceptance criteria plus the quality and release checks common to everything.

The intellectual lineage runs through three traditions that were not, at the time, speaking to each other. Extreme Programming in the late 1990s — Kent Beck’s formulation — held that code was not finished until it was tested and integrated, an attack on the practice of counting unintegrated branches as progress. William Wake’s “done done” (2002) gave the gap a memorable name. Scrum absorbed the idea, and Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland made it explicit in the Scrum Guide around 2010, elevating it in the 2020 revision to a formal commitment attached to the increment, alongside the product goal and the sprint goal. Meanwhile, the lean and flow tradition — Donald Reinertsen’s work on product development flow (2009), and Craig Larman and Bas Vodde’s analysis of scaled Scrum (2008–2010) — supplied the economic argument: unfinished work is inventory, inventory hides defects, and an organisation that systematically defers completion accumulates what Larman and Vodde named, acidly, an “undone department.” The continuous-delivery tradition, from Jez Humble and David Farley’s Continuous Delivery (2010) through the Accelerate research programme of Nicole Forsgren, Humble and Gene Kim (2018), added a different claim: that any completion criterion which is not enforced by an automated pipeline will decay, and that the meaningful unit of done is a deployable artefact, not a satisfied checklist.

These traditions converge on the problem and diverge sharply on the remedy. It is worth setting out what each school would and would not put its name to, because most arguments about done-ness in real companies are arguments between two of these positions held by people who have not noticed they are holding a position at all.

ThreeMechanics in depth, including the parts left implicit

Expert practice follows a sequence that is rarely written down in full. The first move is an inventory: reconstruct, from the last several changes that actually reached customers without incident, everything that had to be true. Done honestly this produces fifteen to twenty-five items and includes several that nobody had ever named — a colleague who always checks the migration on a copy of production data, a support lead who quietly rewrites release notes.

The second move is placement, and it is where most of the value is created. Each inventory item has five possible homes, not two. It may be a per-story acceptance criterion, because it is about the behaviour of one feature. It may be a definition-of-done item, because it applies to all work. It may be a pipeline gate, which is a definition-of-done item that has been automated and therefore costs nothing per story and cannot be forgotten. It may belong on a release checklist, executed once per release rather than once per story — customer release notes, a regulatory filing, a load test against the full release. Or it may belong in an undone-work register: a named, owned, dated list of completion work the team has consciously decided not to do in-sprint, which converts an invisible debt into a visible one.

The placement decision is governed by four tests applied in order. Is the item universal across the work this team does? Is it verifiable by someone other than the author — which disqualifies “the code is clean” and admits “a second engineer has approved the change”? Is it within the team’s control, meaning the team can complete it without entering a queue it does not own? And is it cheap enough to verify every time, which is a real constraint: a seven-item definition of done at five minutes of verification per item costs thirty-five minutes per story, and on a team completing twelve stories a sprint that is a working day a sprint spent checking.

The third move is enforcement design, which practitioners almost always leave implicit and then regret. Three questions need explicit answers before the first sprint. What happens to a story that misses one item — does it stay in progress, and do its points go uncounted? Who may grant a waiver, and is the waiver recorded with a reason and a remediation date? And what happens to the burndown and the velocity series when a story is carried over — because the common practice of claiming partial points for partially done stories destroys the only data the team has about its own capacity.

The second-order effects of a well-enforced definition of done are more interesting than the first-order ones, and expert practitioners choose their items partly for these effects. Because there is no partial credit, teams start splitting stories smaller, since a smaller story is more likely to clear the whole bar within a sprint. Smaller stories reduce work in process, and by Little’s law — lead time equals work in process divided by throughput — reduced work in process shortens lead time even with unchanged throughput. Because the definition is agreed before estimation, estimates rise, which looks like a productivity loss and is in fact the correction of a measurement error. And because waivers are recorded, the organisation acquires a dataset about which parts of its process are chronically unaffordable, which is usually a more valuable artefact than the definition itself.

There is a quantitative treatment, and it is worth working rather than naming, because it answers the question practitioners actually argue about: how strict should the definition be? Let s denote strictness — the fraction of total completion work performed in-sprint, so s = 0 means code-complete-and-move-on and s = 1 means every last check performed on every story. Three costs vary with s, measured in engineer-hours per story point.

The first is the in-sprint cost. It rises with strictness, and it rises convexly, because the last checks — full regression, manual exploratory testing, a performance run — are far more expensive per unit of assurance than the first ones. Model it as 6 + 3s + 9s4 hours per point: six hours of build, a linear component for routine rigour, and a steep term that only bites above about s = 0.8. The second is the deferred cost: the completion work not done in-sprint must still be done, later, at a rework multiplier for lost context and dependent changes. If four hours per point of completion work exists and the multiplier is 2.6, deferred cost is 10.4(1 − s). The third is the escape cost: defects that reach production. Assume nine production incidents per 100 points at s = 0, falling linearly to zero, at 22 hours each — that is 1.98(1 − s) hours per point.
