FourWhen the idea applies, and when it misleads

The conditions under which a definition of done does what it claims can be stated as four testable claims, and it is instructive to apply each to both protagonists.

Claim one: the team can reach a releasable state within one cadence. If it cannot — because a mandatory step takes longer than the sprint — then the definition will be violated structurally and will teach the team that the rules are theatre. At Palash this holds: the three proposed items add hours, not weeks. At Anagha it fails outright for the full regression pack, which takes eleven days of elapsed time across fourteen customer configurations. Sunil cannot put the whole pack in a two-week definition of done no matter how much he wants to.

Claim two: the team bears the cost of its own undone work. Where it does not, the definition is fighting an externality and will lose. Palash’s squads feel the cost of bad instrumentation directly — they are the ones who rebuild the experiment. Anagha’s squads do not: the 340 person-days of remediation were paid by implementation and support, in a different building, against a different budget line. This asymmetry, not laziness, is why Anagha’s definition stopped where it did, and it is why the fix has to be organisational before it can be procedural.

Claim three: verification is cheap relative to the work. A check that costs twenty per cent of a story is not a definition-of-done item, it is a separate activity that needs its own place. This is the practical argument for automation: an automated gate has zero marginal verification cost and infinite consistency.

Claim four: the work is homogeneous enough for one bar. A team doing feature work, defect fixes, spikes and regulated changes with a single definition will either over-constrain the spikes or under-constrain the regulated work. This is the flow school’s point, and it is correct.

There are situations where the idea is not merely inapplicable but actively misleading. A research spike whose output is knowledge should be governed by a time-box and a written finding, not by a completion checklist; imposing one produces a spike that ships code, which is the opposite of what a spike is for. Incident response cannot wait for a peer review at three in the morning, and pretending otherwise generates either dangerous delay or a culture of casual waivers that then spreads. Early-stage discovery work, where most of what is built will be discarded within weeks, gains nothing from migration scripts and runbooks. And in machine-learning work, a binary bar applied to a statistical result is a category error, which the AI section below takes up in detail.

FiveHard edge cases and what mature companies actually do

Platform and multi-product organisations face a question that single-product teams never confront: whether a platform team’s change is done when it is deployed, or only when consuming teams have adopted it. Deployed-but-unadopted platform work is the purest form of hidden inventory, because it looks complete on every board and delivers no value at all; worse, it commits the platform team to maintaining two code paths indefinitely. Mature organisations resolve this by writing migration into the platform’s definition of done — typically as “the change is adopted by at least one consumer in production, and a dated deprecation plan exists for the old path.” What they say they do is “the platform team owns the interface.” What they actually do, on the good teams, is send an engineer to do the first consumer’s migration personally.

Two-sided marketplaces have a supply-side version of the same problem. A change to how sellers are paid is not done when the code ships; it is done when the seller-operations standard operating procedure has been updated, the field team that onboards sellers has been briefed, and the two support macros have been rewritten. Marketplace teams that define done in purely software terms ship changes the operations organisation cannot absorb, and the resulting mess is diagnosed as a product failure when it is a definition failure. The honest marketplace definition of done has a non-engineering item in it, which orthodox Scrum finds uncomfortable and practice demands.

Regulated environments — Sunil’s world, and that of anyone building for banking, insurance, health or payments in India — add evidence as a first-class output. The artefact that satisfies an auditor is not working software but a traceable chain: this requirement, these test cases, this result, this approval, this date. The mature pattern is to make evidence generation a by-product of the pipeline rather than a separate documentation exercise, so that the test run emits the evidence automatically. The immature pattern, which is far more common, is a pre-release week in which people assemble screenshots. The distinction between the two is worth several weeks per release and, more importantly, determines whether the evidence describes what actually happened.

Hardware-plus-software organisations confront date-locked gates that no amount of agility can soften: certification, factory tooling, a firmware image that must be frozen because it is being flashed on a line. Done for firmware and done for the companion application cannot be the same definition, and attempting to unify them produces the worst of both. The workable pattern separates the cadences explicitly and defines a joint integration bar — a version-compatibility matrix that both sides commit to — which is itself an item in each side’s definition of done.

AI-native products break the binary. When acceptance is a measured pass-rate on an evaluation set rather than a boolean, “done” becomes a statistical claim with a confidence interval, and a naive threshold invites self-deception. Consider a support-assistant team — call it the pattern Shravan AI follows — with a frozen evaluation set of 1,200 conversations and a done-bar of 92 per cent rubric pass. A measured 92.6 per cent looks like a pass. But the standard error at p = 0.93 with n = 1,200 is the square root of (0.93 × 0.07 / 1200), which is 0.0074, so the 95 per cent interval is roughly ±1.4 percentage points. A measurement of 92.6 per cent is statistically indistinguishable from 91.2 per cent, which fails. A serious definition of done for such work therefore specifies the evaluation set version, the sample size, and a decision rule stated on the interval rather than the point estimate — typically that the lower bound must exceed the incumbent’s point estimate. It must also handle a property unique to this domain: done can un-done itself when an underlying model is updated beneath you, which is why version pinning and a re-evaluation trigger belong in the definition rather than in somebody’s calendar.

SixThe nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The four-artefact discipline

Competent practitioners distinguish acceptance criteria from the definition of done. Experts run four distinct artefacts — acceptance criteria, definition of ready, definition of done and release checklist — and can say which is which without hesitating. The tell-tale sign in the wild is a definition of done containing feature behaviour, such as “refund amounts are correct.” The obvious reading is that this is a quality item and therefore welcome; the correct reading is that it cannot be universal, so it will be either meaningless or unverifiable on the ninety per cent of stories that have nothing to do with refunds, and its presence trains people to read the list as decorative.

Floor, not ceiling, and only ever ratcheted

The definition of done states the minimum the team will always do, not the standard it aspires to. Experts add items one at a time, after the team has demonstrated it can hold the current bar, and they never add an item in the emotional aftermath of an incident without asking what it displaces. The tell is a definition that grew by one item after every post-mortem and has never lost one.

Automatable or erodes

Any manual item on a definition of done is in a slow race against schedule pressure, and schedule pressure is undefeated. The expert’s working assumption is that a manual check survives about two quarters before it becomes a formality performed without attention. This does not mean manual items are forbidden — a support engineer reading a runbook cannot be automated — but it does mean each manual item should be justified explicitly and reviewed quarterly. The tell is a team that can produce a green checklist for a story whose author admits, when asked privately, that step four was ticked without being done.

The externality test

Before believing any definition of done, an expert asks who pays when an item is skipped. If the answer is a different team, a different budget or a future quarter, the definition will erode regardless of anyone’s intentions, because the party bearing the cost is not the party making the decision. The tell is Anagha’s pattern exactly: a squad with a perfect done-rate and an implementation organisation working weekends.

The waiver economy

Every real definition has exceptions. What distinguishes a healthy team is that waivers are recorded, attributed and counted. Experts look at the waiver rate before they look at the list: below roughly one story in twenty, the definition is real; above one in five, the team has a fiction and a second, unwritten definition that is the one actually in force. The tell is that nobody can answer the question “how many exceptions did we grant last quarter?”

Increment-level done versus story-level done

Some items only make sense at the level of the increment or the release: end-to-end tests across several stories, a performance run, a security scan of the assembled system. Insisting on them per story is wasteful; omitting them entirely is dangerous. Experts run a two-tier structure and are explicit about which tier each item belongs to. The tell is a team arguing about whether load testing belongs in the definition of done, where both sides are right about different tiers.

Carry-over accounting

What a team does with a story that is 80 per cent complete at the sprint boundary determines whether its velocity series means anything. Claiming partial points converts the velocity number into a measure of effort rather than completion, at which point it can no longer be used for forecasting — which is the only thing it was for. Experts carry the whole story and count nothing, accept the lumpy series, and use a rolling average. The tell is a suspiciously smooth velocity chart.

Done as a distribution

In data and machine-learning work, and increasingly in anything with a model in the path, done is not a boolean but a claim about a distribution, with a sample size and an interval. Experts write the evaluation set version, the sample size and the decision rule into the definition. The tell is a bare percentage threshold with no n beside it.

The observability clause

An item that reliably earns its place in mature definitions is some version of “we can tell from production whether this is working.” It is unusual among completion items in that its value is realised entirely after the sprint. The expert’s reason for including it is not hygiene but optionality: a change you can observe is a change you can safely reverse, and reversibility is what allows everything else to move faster. Aparna’s three proposed items are all, at bottom, this one item.

Locality

Definitions of done travel badly. A list that works for a payments team with a two-week regulatory review cycle is wrong for a growth team running four experiments a week, and copying it produces a checklist nobody believes. The tell is a definition of done that arrived by email from a central agile function, identical across nine teams, with an item referring to a tool one of them does not use.

SevenDifferences by product type and company stage

In consumer products the centre of gravity sits on reversibility and measurement, for the straightforward reason that release frequency is high and the cost of any individual defect is usually low, while the cost of an unmeasurable release is total. In B2B and enterprise it sits on compatibility, migration, documentation and support readiness, because customers run old versions, integrate through interfaces that must not break, and reach a human being when things go wrong. In platforms it sits on adoption and deprecation. In marketplaces it extends beyond software into operational readiness. In hardware-adjacent products it is dominated by date-locked external gates. In AI products it becomes statistical and must handle the fact that the ground can move underneath a completed story.

What does not differ, and is often claimed to, is the underlying discipline. It is sometimes said that consumer teams need lighter definitions than enterprise ones. The evidence does not support the generalisation: a consumer team shipping ten times a day has more of its completion work in the pipeline, not less, and its definition of done is often longer than an enterprise team’s once you count the automated gates. The real variable is not product type but release frequency and blast radius, and product type is merely a correlate of both.

Company stage matters in a specific and limited way. At pre-product-market-fit scale, where most of what is built will be deleted within two months, a deliberately thin definition — three or four items — is correct, and rigour applied to disposable code is waste. What a young company must not do is have no definition, because even there the gap between “it demonstrates” and “a customer can use it unattended” is the difference between a real signal and a false one, and false signals at that stage are fatal. At scale the failure is the mirror image: definitions accrete, one item per incident, until the list is a liturgy that everyone waives. Mature organisations prune deliberately, usually by automating what can be automated and demoting the rest, and they treat the size of the list as a metric in its own right.

EightThree worked examples, including one failure

Palash Money: instrumentation as a completion item. Aparna adopted the three items on 1 October 2025 for two of her three squads, holding the third unchanged as a comparison. Over the following quarter the treated squads’ throughput fell from 46 to 42 points per sprint — a nine per cent decline, exactly as estimated. Experiment usability, measured by the data team on the same rubric as the H1 audit, rose from 68 per cent to 94 per cent. On 34 experiments in the quarter that is a shift from roughly eleven unusable experiments to two, saving about nine × 9.5 = 86 engineer-days, or ₹15.4 lakh, against a throughput cost of roughly nine per cent of two squads’ capacity — about 58 engineer-days, ₹10.4 lakh. The direct financial case was positive but not overwhelming. The decisive effect was elsewhere: median time from experiment launch to a decision the leadership would act on fell from 5.5 weeks to 3.0 weeks, because nobody was re-running experiments to fix the tracking. Aparna’s retrospective judgement was that she had bought decision latency and paid for it in throughput, and that she had mispriced the trade for a year by measuring only the latter.

Anagha Insurance Technologies: moving the seam, not erasing it. Sunil did not try to put 3,100 regression cases into a sprint, which would have failed claim one above. Instead his team ran a change-impact analysis mapping each module to the subset of cases that could plausibly be affected, and found that 420 cases — 13.5 per cent — covered the modules responsible for 31 of the 41 June defects. Those 420 were automated over seven weeks by four engineers, a cost of 28 person-weeks or roughly ₹24.6 lakh, and added to the squads’ definition of done as a pipeline gate running against three representative customer configurations. Post-upgrade defects at the following two upgrades fell from 41 to 12 and from 12 to 9, severity-one from nine to one, and implementation and support effort per upgrade from 340 to 95 person-days. At a blended ₹17,600 per person-day that is ₹43 lakh per upgrade, so the automation paid for itself inside the first upgrade. The remaining 2,680 cases stayed exactly where they were, on the release checklist, owned by implementation — which is the point. The improvement came from moving the seam thirteen per cent to the left with evidence, not from pretending the seam did not exist.

NineFailure modes and their early diagnostics

The inherited definition. The early warning sign is that the list arrived from outside the team and no member can explain why a particular item is on it. The diagnostic question is simply “which of these items would you block a release for at 6 p.m. on a Friday?” — the items nobody names are already dead. Caught early, the fix is an afternoon; caught late, it is Chirag’s two lost quarters.

The unbounded ratchet. The warning sign is a definition that has grown monotonically, one item per incident. The diagnostic is to ask when an item was last removed; if the answer is never, the list is a memorial rather than a standard. The cost of catching this late is the slow, unattributable throughput decline that eventually gets blamed on hiring.

Structural non-compliance. The warning sign is chronic carry-over attributed to other teams. The diagnostic is to name, for each item, the person who can complete it; any item whose name is outside the team is a structural defect in the definition, not a performance problem in the team. Late detection costs trust, because it teaches a team that the rules do not apply to it.

Silent waiver drift. The warning sign is a rising number of stories that are done but followed within a week by a small unplanned fix. The diagnostic is to count waivers and, if none are recorded, to look instead at the ratio of unplanned to planned work. Late detection is expensive because the drift is invisible on every dashboard until an incident.

Done-as-quality substitution. The warning sign is leadership quoting done-rate as a quality metric. The diagnostic is to ask what the definition would have caught in the last three production incidents; the usual answer is none of them, because incidents typically arise from things no checklist covers — capacity, third-party failure, a misunderstanding of a requirement. Catching this late means an organisation that believes it has controlled a risk it has not.

Outcome blindness. The warning sign is a team with an immaculate definition of done and no view of whether anything it ships is used. The diagnostic is to pick three features completed last quarter and ask what changed as a result. This is the failure mode the outcome-first school exists to name, and it is the most expensive of all, because everything else on this list is a way of building the wrong thing more reliably.

TenWhere experts genuinely disagree

Checklist or pipeline? The continuous-delivery position, in its strongest form, is that a definition of done which is not executable is a statement of intent and will be honoured in proportion to how convenient it is; the evidence is the consistent finding across the DevOps research programmes that automated deployment gates correlate with both lower change-failure rates and faster delivery, and the everyday observation that manual checks decay. The strongest counter-position holds that the most valuable completion items are precisely the ones that cannot be automated — a human reading a runbook, a designer looking at the thing on a real phone, an engineer asking whether the error message makes sense to a store manager in Erode — and that automating the automatable and dropping the rest quietly optimises for the measurable. What would have to be true for the automation position to be wrong: that teams with predominantly manual definitions sustain low waiver rates over years. Such teams exist, and they are almost always small, stable and unusually senior, which tells you the condition under which the counter-position holds.

Team-owned or organisation-mandated? Orthodox Scrum insists the team owns its definition, on the argument that a standard imposed from outside is complied with rather than believed, and that only the team knows what completion really takes. The assurance school insists that in regulated or safety-relevant domains the floor is set externally and is not negotiable, on the argument that the cost of a failure is borne by people who are not in the room. Both are right within their domains, and the genuinely contested territory is the middle: a payments company that is not formally regulated in a particular activity but would be ruined by a breach. The practical settlement most mature companies reach — an organisational floor of three to five items, with everything above it owned by the team — is a compromise, not a synthesis, and the argument about where the floor sits recurs annually.

One definition or several? The flow school’s position is that classes of service differ enough that a single bar necessarily over-constrains some work and under-constrains the rest, and it points to the observable fact that teams already behave this way informally when handling incidents. The orthodox position is that multiple definitions are an invitation to route work into the cheapest class, and that the simplicity of one bar is itself the mechanism. The evidence here is weak on both sides, and honest practitioners choose by temperament and by how much they trust their own organisation not to game a classification.

Is “done” even the right unit? The outcome-first school holds that the entire apparatus measures output and that a team can achieve a hundred per cent done-rate while moving nothing. The completion school’s reply is not that outcomes do not matter but that outcome measurement is slow, noisy and often unattributable, whereas completion is fast, clean and controllable — and that a team which cannot reliably finish things has no hope of achieving outcomes anyway. The positions are compatible in principle and rivalrous in practice, because they compete for the same attention in the same rituals. What would falsify the outcome-first critique: evidence that teams with strong completion discipline do not, on average, achieve better outcomes than teams without it. What would falsify the completion school: a demonstration that done-rate improvements routinely occur without any corresponding change in customer-visible reliability — which is, uncomfortably, exactly what Chirag’s middle row shows.

Do performance budgets belong in it? A narrower but persistent argument. One camp says a non-functional budget — the page renders in under two seconds on a mid-range Android device over a 4G connection — is the only defence against the slow degradation that no single change is responsible for. The other says such budgets are properly acceptance criteria for the stories that touch performance-sensitive paths, and that checking them on every story is a tax paid mostly by stories that could not possibly affect them. The resolution depends on whether the team has cheap automated measurement; where it does, the first camp is plainly right, and where it does not, the second camp is describing reality.

ElevenWhat mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in four observable ways. First, they ask about done-ness before estimating, not after building, so that the definition is embedded in every commitment the team makes rather than applied as a judgement afterwards. Second, they are more interested in the waiver log than in the definition; they know that the list on the wall is an aspiration and the exception record is the truth. Third, they think in placements rather than in binaries — confronted with a completion item that will not fit, they move it to a named home with an owner and a date instead of arguing about whether it is really necessary. Fourth, and most distinctively, they are willing to make the definition weaker. A practitioner who has only studied the topic treats every proposed addition as a win; someone who has internalised it knows that both ends of the strictness curve cost the same, and that deleting an unverifiable item is as much of an improvement as adding a verifiable one.

There is a fifth marker, subtler than the rest. Experts use the definition of done as a commercial instrument. When a sales director asks for three weeks off a date, the master practitioner does not argue about effort; they open the definition and ask which of these nine checks the business would like to purchase the omission of, and who will carry the consequence. That conversation is impossible without a written definition and nearly automatic with one. It is also the doorway to the next topic in this sequence — negotiating quality bars and cut lines — because a definition of done converts a vague argument about speed into a specific, priced menu of risks.

TwelveWhat each protagonist decided

Aparna adopted all three items, but not on the schedule her engineer proposed. She held the quarter’s board commitment, absorbed the nine per cent by cutting one roadmap item rather than by hoping, and staged the rollout across two squads with the third as a control so that she would have evidence rather than an anecdote by January. Her reasoning was that the three items were not quality items at all but decision-latency items: Palash’s competitive position depended on the rate at which it could learn, and a third of its experiments had been producing no learning. She also did something less obvious — she added the definition to the template her squads used when proposing an experiment, so that the analysis plan and the event schema were written on the same day, which removed the most common root cause without adding any check at all.

Sunil declined to extend his squads’ definition of done to the full regression pack, on the grounds that it would have been violated structurally within one sprint and would have destroyed the credibility of everything else on the list. He funded the change-impact analysis and the 420-case automation instead, moved the seam thirteen per cent leftwards, and — the part that mattered most and took the longest — he moved the implementation organisation’s remediation cost on to the product budget line, so that the squads bore the consequence of their own undone work. The procedural change was the small half of the fix. The budgetary change was the large half, and it took two quarters and an uncomfortable conversation with a finance director.

Discussion question one. Exhibit 2 shows that a maximal definition of done costs almost exactly what no definition costs. If that is true, why do organisations so reliably drift towards the maximal end rather than the minimal one, and what mechanism would you install to counteract the drift?

Discussion question two. Sunil fixed an incentive before he fixed a process. Under what circumstances is a definition of done simply the wrong instrument — that is, when is the real problem that the wrong party bears the cost of undone work, and how would you recognise that situation from the outside?

Discussion question three. Chirag’s 23-item definition reduced throughput by 39 per cent and did not reduce escaped defects at all. Construct the strongest possible defence of the delivery manager who introduced it, and then say precisely which piece of evidence would have changed your mind in month two rather than month nine.

ThirteenGoing deeper

Acceptance criteria and error cases is the foundation this topic rests on, and the place to go next if any part of the distinction above felt slippery. A definition of done is only as valuable as the per-story criteria it supplements: most of the defects in all three worked examples were in error cases that nobody had written down, which no universal checklist can catch.

Negotiating quality bars and cut lines is what a definition of done unlocks. Once completion is written down, the argument with a customer or an executive stops being about effort and becomes a priced menu: here is the specific check you are asking us to skip, here is what it protects, here is who pays if it fails.

The software development lifecycle supplies the map on which all of this sits — where requirements, build, verification, release and operation actually happen in a given organisation. Without that map, placement decisions are guesswork, because you cannot route an item to a home you have not named.

Agile in practice matters here mostly as an antidote. The best teaching on this module warns explicitly against too much agile mechanics, and the definition of done is the most frequently ritualised artefact in the canon; studying how agile actually behaves in working organisations is the best protection against treating the list as the point.

Kanban and flow supplies the economics that justify the whole argument: work in process, Little’s law, batch size and the treatment of undone work as inventory. It is also where the strongest intellectual challenge to a single team-wide definition comes from, in the form of class-of-service policies.

The execution rhythm determines how often the definition is tested and how quickly a violation becomes visible. Cadence and strictness are coupled, as Exhibit 2’s second pass demonstrated: change the release frequency and the optimal definition changes with it.

Engineering estimates and T-shirt sizing becomes meaningful only once done is defined, since an estimate is an estimate of reaching a state, and a team that does not agree on the state is not disagreeing about numbers at all. Most estimation disputes dissolve when the definition is written down.

Backlog management and refinement is where the definition is applied in advance: a well-refined item is one whose path to satisfying the definition is already understood, which is why refinement quality and done-rate move together in almost every team that measures both.
